title: Detect Gatekeeper Bypass via Quarantine Flag and Trust Control Manipulation
shortTitle: Detect Gatekeeper Bypass via Quarantine Flag and Trust Co...
summary: This strategy detects attempts to bypass the macOS Gatekeeper control that evaluates downloaded software before it is allowed to run. Adversaries, and some unwanted installers, do this by stripping the quarantine attribute from a downloaded file, by changing the system policy that decides which software may run, or by approving unsigned code directly, all of which weaken a core platform control instead of exploiting a flaw. The enabling telemetry is endpoint process execution with full arguments, unified log entries from the system policy and assessment subsystem, file attribute change records for the quarantine flag, and configuration inventory for the assessment setting. It fails when the sensor does not record command arguments, because the very same trusted utilities service ordinary software installation and then produce byte for byte identical process names.

beginner.definition: Gatekeeper is a safety check built into macOS. When you download a program from the internet, the system marks the file. It then asks an approval question before the program can run. Some attackers remove that mark, or weaken the check, so their program runs with no prompt at all. This detection watches for changes to that protection.
beginner.whyItMatters: This control protects every downloaded program on the machine, not just one file. Once it is weakened, unsigned or unwanted software can run quietly for a long time. The tools that change it are normal system tools. A rule based on tool names alone will not help you. Because the change is rare and deliberate, a good alert here is usually worth investigating.
howItWorks: The macOS sensor records every process that runs, together with the arguments passed to it.
The rule keeps the commands that manage this protection, such as the ones that edit file attributes or system policy.
It reads the arguments to see whether the command removes the download mark or changes the assessment setting.
Log entries from the assessment subsystem confirm that the policy changed, and they name the calling process.
Configuration inventory shows the protection state of each host, so an unexpected change stands out from the baseline.
The analyst checks which program was approved or run in the minutes right after the change.
beginner.example: Think of a building with a guard at the main door who checks every visitor. Someone finds a way to switch off the guard's badge reader and then walks straight in. From outside, the door still looks completely normal. Your detection watches the badge reader itself, because a reader that has been switched off is the real clue.
takeaways: This is a change to a protection control, so it is rare and usually deliberate.
Read the command arguments, because the tool names themselves are completely normal.
Note which program ran after the change, since that is the payload you actually care about.

objectives: Explain what Gatekeeper protects and when it makes an evaluation decision.
Recognise command arguments that remove the quarantine mark from a downloaded file.
Interpret unified log entries that report a change to the assessment policy.
Correlate a protection change with the program that runs immediately afterwards.
Use configuration inventory to catch the same change made through a management tool.
dataSources: macOS Endpoint Security process execution events with full arguments, signing information and the responsible parent process
macOS unified log entries from the system policy and assessment subsystem recording protection state changes
Endpoint file attribute or extended attribute change records for the download quarantine flag
Mobile device management or configuration profile inventory showing the Gatekeeper assessment setting for each host
logic: The pattern is a trusted system utility being used to remove or weaken the platform control that evaluates downloaded software. The fields to correlate are the process path and its full argument list from execution telemetry, the effective user, the responsible parent process, and the corresponding change recorded by the assessment subsystem or the configuration inventory for that host. The benign case is a software deployment agent or an administrator installing an internally built package from a managed repository, where the same action repeats across many hosts and the file being approved is signed and comes from a known internal share. The malicious case is a one off attribute removal on a file in a downloads or temporary directory, a policy change that disables the check, or an approval granted to an unsigned file that has no history anywhere in the estate.
pseudoQuery:
# title: Gatekeeper Quarantine Removal or Assessment Disabled
# logsource:
#   product: macos
# detection:
#   selection:
#     process_name|endswith:
#       - '/xattr'
#       - '/spctl'
#     command_line|contains:
#       - 'com.apple.quarantine'
#       - '--master-disable'
#       - '--add'
#   filter:
#     command_line|contains: '/Applications/Managed/'
#   condition: selection and not filter
# level: medium
falsePositives: Software deployment agents that install internally built packages from a managed repository and clear the download mark first.
Developers running locally built binaries during testing and removing the quarantine attribute themselves.
Administrators approving an internally signed application through the policy tool during workstation onboarding.
Backup or migration tools that copy application bundles between machines and adjust their file attributes.
tuningNotes: Baseline which processes touch the quarantine attribute across managed Macs for two weeks, then filter the deployment agent and its managed repository path rather than the command name. Scope the high severity branch to Macs that handle sensitive data, and keep engineering machines, where developers clear the attribute on their own builds, at low severity with the arguments retained for review. Leave the policy change condition unfiltered, because disabling the assessment setting is rare and almost never legitimate outside a documented change record. Filtering by deployment path costs coverage of an attacker who abuses the approved deployment agent, so add a separate alert for that agent when it is invoked interactively outside a scheduled deployment window.
